screens.title: Interacting with Solana via the CLI
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will master the Solana command line interface, the essential tool for direct blockchain interactions. The CLI lets you pick which Solana cluster to use, tell the tool which wallet file should sign transactions, request development airdrops, and move native SOL between accounts. Learning the CLI accelerates testing and debugging because it gives you low-level visibility into transactions, signatures, and program logs. For example, you can configure your terminal to devnet, request two SOL for testing, and then transfer a small amount to a temporary account, all without a browser. We will also cover how to inspect transaction details and common mistakes like forgetting to set the correct cluster or not accounting for fees. By the end of these screens you will be able to switch cluster contexts reliably, verify balances, handle transfers that create new accounts, and use the confirm and transaction commands to debug your operations. Keep the CLI habits tight: always verify your configuration, check balances before sending, and examine signatures when things go wrong.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Interacting with Solana via the CLI
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Command Line Access to Solana

Use the Solana CLI to control cluster connections, wallet keypairs, request test airdrops, move SOL, and inspect transaction details for debugging and development.

Why this matters: the CLI removes UI friction and surfaces raw transaction data and logs you need when the program behavior differs from expectation.

Concrete example: configure the CLI to devnet, request 2 SOL, transfer 0.1 SOL to a temporary keypair, then inspect the transaction signature to confirm state changes.

Misconception check: the CLI’s airdrops are available only on devnet, testnet, and localhost — never on mainnet-beta.

Inspect

Inspect

Explore Key Topics

Keypairs — set your default signer to avoid accidental mainnet use.
Transaction inspection — confirm and transaction reveal logs and instructions.

screens.title: What is the Solana CLI?
screens.narratorSegment: The Solana CLI is a command-line tool that gives you direct access to the Solana network and node APIs without a graphical interface. It’s a concise set of commands for configuring network targets, managing keypairs, requesting test SOL, sending transactions, and inspecting the resulting signatures and logs. For a developer, the CLI is crucial because it exposes the low-level details you need when a program behaves unexpectedly. For example, if a deployed program fails, the CLI’s transaction output shows instruction ordering, account changes, and program logs you can use to locate the bug. The CLI also avoids the latency and abstraction of browser-based wallets during development: you can run repeatable scripts and capture raw outputs. A common misconception is that the CLI is only for advanced users; in truth, it is the most reliable way to validate program logic and to automate routine tasks during development. Knowing the CLI commands will help you reproduce issues reliably and move faster when building and debugging your Solana programs. What is the Solana CLI? means the cli exposes raw network and transaction details developers need for precise testing, debugging, and automation.. In practical terms, definition and why it's crucial for development. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › What is the Solana CLI?
Definition

A developer tool for direct network access

The CLI provides commands to set cluster targets, choose a signing keypair, request development funds, execute transfers, deploy programs, and inspect transactions for logs and account changes.

Key capabilities
  • Configure cluster URL and default keypair.
  • Request airdrops on devnet, testnet, and localhost.
  • Send SOL transfers and inspect transaction details.
Common misconception

The CLI is not only for experts; it's the fastest way to reproduce and debug program behavior because it reveals raw transaction data and logs.

Analogy
The CLI is like a microscope for blockchain operations

It magnifies low-level details you cannot see in a wallet UI and helps you diagnose why a transaction or program instruction failed.

Example
Check cluster version
solana cluster-version
# Example output:
# 1.18.15 (solana-release v1.18.15)

screens.title: Configuring the CLI: clusters and keypairs
screens.narratorSegment: Configuration is the first step every time you open a new terminal for Solana development. You must set the cluster URL so commands run against the intended network, and set the default keypair file used for signing. Typical clusters are mainnet-beta, devnet, testnet, or localhost. The commands are explicit: use the set command with --url to pick the cluster and --keypair to point to a wallet file. After setting, always run solana config get to confirm your context. A common trap is assuming the terminal is already configured for devnet or localhost. If you accidentally send a transaction to mainnet-beta, recovery is difficult. As a concrete example, set your CLI to devnet and then set a specific keypair file. Verify with config get. Practice habit: verify URL and keypair before any transfer command. This avoids wrong-cluster mistakes and ensures your signature is produced from the correct wallet file. Configuring the CLI: clusters and keypairs means always configure --url and --keypair (or confirm with solana config get) before performing network actions to avoid wrong-cluster mistakes.. In practical terms, set the target cluster and default signer reliably. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Configuring the CLI
Commands

Set cluster and keypair

Use solana config set with --url to change clusters and --keypair to choose which wallet signs transactions. Always run solana config get afterwards.

# Set the cluster to Devnet
solana config set --url devnet

# Set your default keypair
essolana config set --keypair /path/to/your/devnet-wallet.json

# Verify configuration
solana config get
Why confirm

solana config get shows your current URL and keypair. This explicit confirmation prevents accidental operations on mainnet-beta or another unintended cluster.

Concrete tip

When scripting, prefer passing --url and --keypair in the command so the script is explicit about its target, rather than relying on global config.

Key Takeaway

Always confirm your cluster and signer. Mistaken context is the most common source of surprising CLI behavior.

screens.title: Using solana config get and cluster-version
screens.narratorSegment: Two verification commands you will use constantly are solana config get and solana cluster-version. The first prints the CLI’s current URL, keypair path, and other runtime settings. Use it whenever you open a new terminal or before running a script. The second returns the cluster’s software version string that indicates the node release you're talking to. This is useful for debugging compatibility issues or confirming network health. For example, if you see that your cluster is running an older release, it may explain why a newer program feature fails. Running these commands is straightforward: config get prints your local settings, while cluster-version queries the connected RPC and returns a version line. Remember that cluster-version tests reachability and gives you a sense of the network's update status. Use these checks as part of your pre-flight checklist before requesting airdrops or sending transactions. Using solana config get and cluster-version means run solana config get and solana cluster-version to confirm your cli context and the network software version before making changes.. In practical terms, verify network version and your cli context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Verify context & version
Command

solana config get

Use this to confirm your CLI's current URL and default keypair path. It prevents accidental use of the wrong cluster or signer.

solana config get
# Example output:
# RPC URL: https://api.devnet.solana.com
# Keypair Path: /home/user/.config/solana/devnet-wallet.json
# Commitment: confirmed
Command

solana cluster-version

Queries the node for its release version. Helpful when debugging compatibility or node-specific behavior.

solana cluster-version
# Example output:
# 1.18.15 (solana-release v1.18.15)
Key Takeaway

Make these checks part of your pre-flight routine to detect wrong contexts and node incompatibilities early.

screens.title: Requesting Airdrops on Devnet and Localhost
screens.narratorSegment: Airdrops let you obtain test SOL quickly on devnet, testnet, or localhost, which is essential for prototyping without real funds. The solana airdrop command requests the specified amount of SOL for your default keypair or for a provided public key. On devnet, airdrops are generally modest; on localhost they can be generous and instantaneous. Remember: airdrops are not available on mainnet-beta. When requesting, you will see a request message and a signature confirming the transfer. After the airdrop completes, confirm your balance with solana balance. If you need to fund a different account, pass the account's public key to the airdrop command. Use this workflow when setting up temporary test accounts, or when running local program tests that require funds in multiple accounts. Habit tip: always confirm the returned signature and then check the balance, so you know the network actually processed the request. Requesting Airdrops on Devnet and Localhost means use solana airdrop to fund devnet or localhost accounts for development; always verify the signature and the resulting balance.. In practical terms, get test sol to fund development accounts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Requesting Airdrops
Commands

solana airdrop

Request test SOL for the default keypair or a specified public key. Use on devnet, testnet, or localhost only.

# Request 2 SOL for default keypair on Devnet
solana airdrop 2

# Request 2 SOL for a specific public key
solana airdrop 2 <PUBLIC_KEY_OF_ACCOUNT>
Verify

After the airdrop completes, copy the returned signature and run solana balance to confirm the funds arrived and the account balance updated.

Localhost note

When running solana-test-validator, airdrops are immediate and can be requested in larger amounts for local testing, making it ideal for program state experiments.

Key Takeaway

Use airdrops on devnet or localhost to fund development accounts; confirm signature and balance afterwards.

screens.title: Checking Balances and Recipient Options
screens.narratorSegment: Checking an account’s balance is an essential precondition before sending SOL. The solana balance command reports the SOL for your default keypair or for any public key you supply. When transferring SOL, you must account for transaction fees in addition to the transfer amount. A common situation is sending to a new account that doesn't exist on-chain yet: by default, the transfer may fail because the recipient is not rent-exempt. The CLI provides --allow-unfunded-recipient to create the recipient account automatically as part of the transfer by using a portion of the transferred SOL to pay rent exemption. Use this flag intentionally: it trades clarity for convenience by absorbing rent costs into the transfer. Practically, check the sender balance, compute transfer plus estimated fee, and use the flag only when you expect to create a new account. This comparison clarifies when to require explicit account creation versus permitting the transfer to create the recipient. Checking Balances and Recipient Options means always check balances and include transaction fees; use --allow-unfunded-recipient when you want the transfer to create a new recipient account automatically.. In practical terms, balance checks and the allow-unfunded-recipient flag. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Balance & Recipient Options
Command

solana balance

Check the balance for your default keypair or a supplied public key to ensure sufficient funds for transfers and fees.

# Default keypair
solana balance

# Specific public key
solana balance <PUBLIC_KEY>
Flag

--allow-unfunded-recipient

When sending to a new address, this flag instructs the system to create the recipient account using part of the transfer to pay rent-exemption, avoiding a failed transaction.

# Transfer 0.1 SOL and allow creating the recipient
solana transfer <RECIPIENT_PUBLIC_KEY> 0.1 --allow-unfunded-recipient
Key Takeaway

Always ensure your balance covers the transfer and the fee. Use the flag only when you intentionally want the transfer to create the recipient account.

screens.title: Transferring SOL and interpreting output
screens.narratorSegment: Transferring SOL with the CLI is simple but precise. Use the solana transfer command, specify the recipient public key, the amount, and optionally the --allow-unfunded-recipient flag when sending to a new account. The command returns a transaction signature which you should copy and use for confirmation or inspection. The output typically shows a request, a signature, and the transfer amount. After sending, run solana confirm with the signature if you want to wait for confirmation status, or directly run solana transaction to see instruction-level details. Be careful to include fees in your calculations. For example, sending 0.1 SOL requires more than 0.1 SOL in the sender to cover the fee. If the transfer fails, the CLI output and subsequent transaction details will help you identify whether the error was insufficient funds or a different issue. Practicing this workflow will make routine transfers reliable and debuggable. Transferring SOL and interpreting output means every transfer returns a signature; use it to confirm and inspect the transaction for deterministic debugging.. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Transferring SOL
Command

solana transfer

Run a transfer and capture the signature to confirm or inspect the transaction afterwards.

# Transfer 0.1 SOL to a recipient, creating the recipient if needed
solana transfer <RECIPIENT_PUBLIC_KEY> 0.1 --allow-unfunded-recipient

# After the command you will see a signature; copy it for the next step.
Confirm

Use solana confirm with the signature to wait for network confirmation. This ensures the transaction reached the desired commitment level.

# Wait for confirmation
solana confirm <TRANSACTION_SIGNATURE>
Key Takeaway

Always copy your transaction signature and use it to confirm and inspect the transaction for reliable debugging.

screens.title: Inspecting Transactions with solana transaction
screens.narratorSegment: When you have a transaction signature, solana transaction provides a detailed, raw view of what happened on chain. It prints instructions, account changes, and program logs that are invaluable when a program misbehaves. Use it after solana confirm or on a confirmed signature to examine the instruction sequence and any runtime logs printed by your program. If a transaction fails, transaction output often contains error messages or stack traces showing which instruction caused the failure. screens.title: Common CLI Errors and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: You will encounter a handful of frequent CLI errors while developing. The three common classes are wrong-cluster context, insufficient funds, and missing account rent-exemption. Wrong-cluster errors happen when --url or the global config points to a different network; you may query an address on mainnet-beta while expecting devnet results. Insufficient funds occurs when the sender balance does not cover transfer plus fee. And rent-exemption issues occur when sending to new accounts without the allow-unfunded-recipient flag or without previously creating and funding the account. Troubleshooting follows a short checklist: first run solana config get to verify URL and keypair; second run solana balance for the sender; third copy the transaction signature and use solana transaction to inspect logs. A practical tip is to include explicit --url and --keypair flags in scripts to make behavior deterministic. These steps let you quickly identify whether the problem is configuration, funding, or program logic. Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Localhost Lab
Lab steps
  1. Start the local validator with solana-test-validator and keep it running.
  2. In a new terminal set CLI to localhost: solana config set --url localhost.
  3. Generate and set a keypair: solana-keygen new --outfile localhost-wallet.json and solana config set --keypair localhost-wallet.json.

  5. Create a recipient and transfer 50 SOL with allow-unfunded-recipient, then inspect the signature with solana transaction.
Command examples
# Start validator (keep open)

# Configure CLI for localhost
solana config set --url localhost

# Check balance
solana balance

# Generate recipient and transfer

solana transaction <YOUR_TRANSACTION_SIGNATURE>

The localhost lab is the safest, fastest loop to validate transfers and program state without network variability.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will master the Solana command line interface, the essential tool for direct blockchain interactions. The CLI lets you pick which Solana cluster to use, tell the tool which wallet file should sign transactions, request development airdrops, and move native SOL between accounts. Learning the CLI accelerates testing and debugging because it gives you low-level visibility into transactions, signatures, and program logs. For example, you can configure your terminal to devnet, request two SOL for testing, and then transfer a small amount to a temporary account, all without a browser. We will also cover how to inspect transaction details and common mistakes like forgetting to set the correct cluster or not accounting for fees. By the end of these screens you will be able to switch cluster contexts reliably, verify balances, handle transfers that create new accounts, and use the confirm and transaction commands to debug your operations. Keep the CLI habits tight: always verify your configuration, check balances before sending, and examine signatures when things go wrong.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure the Solana CLI for specific clusters, manage keypairs for signing, perform network interactions like requesting airdrops and checking balances, execute transfers of native SOL, and inspect transactions for debugging. Each objective trains a practical skill: cluster configuration prevents accidental work on the wrong network; keypair management ensures correct transaction signing; requesting and understanding airdrops lets you prototype without cost; transfers and flags teach how to handle new recipient accounts; and transaction inspection reveals low-level logs for troubleshooting. For example, you'll practice configuring the CLI to localhost, generating a new keypair, requesting 100 SOL via a localhost airdrop, then transferring funds to a new recipient and inspecting the resulting transaction signature. We'll also emphasize common errors you might see and how to resolve them quickly. These objectives prepare you to use the CLI reliably during development and testing.

These second objectives focus on hands-on practices and understanding common CLI errors you will encounter. You will learn to request an airdrop on devnet or localhost, interpret the airdrop response, and verify balance changes. You will practice transferring SOL with the allow-unfunded-recipient option and learn when that flag is necessary. Additionally, you will learn to inspect transaction signatures for logs and instruction details, which are key for debugging program errors. A critical skill is troubleshooting: common mistakes include forgetting to set the correct URL or keypair, and not accounting for transaction fees when sending small amounts. For each objective we provide a small mnemonic or quick check to avoid those traps. By practicing these tasks you reduce the chance of accidental mainnet operations and you'll be able to debug failed transactions quickly and confidently.

The Solana CLI is a command-line tool that gives you direct access to the Solana network and node APIs without a graphical interface. It’s a concise set of commands for configuring network targets, managing keypairs, requesting test SOL, sending transactions, and inspecting the resulting signatures and logs. For a developer, the CLI is crucial because it exposes the low-level details you need when a program behaves unexpectedly. For example, if a deployed program fails, the CLI’s transaction output shows instruction ordering, account changes, and program logs you can use to locate the bug. The CLI also avoids the latency and abstraction of browser-based wallets during development: you can run repeatable scripts and capture raw outputs. A common misconception is that the CLI is only for advanced users; in truth, it is the most reliable way to validate program logic and to automate routine tasks during development. Knowing the CLI commands will help you reproduce issues reliably and move faster when building and debugging your Solana programs. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Configuration is the first step every time you open a new terminal for Solana development. You must set the cluster URL so commands run against the intended network, and set the default keypair file used for signing. Typical clusters are mainnet-beta, devnet, testnet, or localhost. The commands are explicit: use the set command with --url to pick the cluster and --keypair to point to a wallet file. After setting, always run solana config get to confirm your context. A common trap is assuming the terminal is already configured for devnet or localhost. If you accidentally send a transaction to mainnet-beta, recovery is difficult. As a concrete example, set your CLI to devnet and then set a specific keypair file. Verify with config get. Practice habit: verify URL and keypair before any transfer command. This avoids wrong-cluster mistakes and ensures your signature is produced from the correct wallet file. Two verification commands you will use constantly are solana config get and solana cluster-version. The first prints the CLI’s current URL, keypair path, and other runtime settings. Use it whenever you open a new terminal or before running a script. The second returns the cluster’s software version string that indicates the node release you're talking to. This is useful for debugging compatibility issues or confirming network health. For example, if you see that your cluster is running an older release, it may explain why a newer program feature fails. Running these commands is straightforward: config get prints your local settings, while cluster-version queries the connected RPC and returns a version line. Remember that cluster-version tests reachability and gives you a sense of the network's update status. Airdrops let you obtain test SOL quickly on devnet, testnet, or localhost, which is essential for prototyping without real funds. The solana airdrop command requests the specified amount of SOL for your default keypair or for a provided public key. When requesting, you will see a request message and a signature confirming the transfer. After the airdrop completes, confirm your balance with solana balance. If you need to fund a different account, pass the account's public key to the airdrop command. You will encounter a handful of frequent CLI errors while developing. The three common classes are wrong-cluster context, insufficient funds, and missing account rent-exemption. Wrong-cluster errors happen when --url or the global config points to a different network; you may query an address on mainnet-beta while expecting devnet results. Insufficient funds occurs when the sender balance does not cover transfer plus fee. And rent-exemption issues occur when sending to new accounts without the allow-unfunded-recipient flag or without previously creating and funding the account. Troubleshooting follows a short checklist: first run solana config get to verify URL and keypair; second run solana balance for the sender; third copy the transaction signature and use solana transaction to inspect logs. A practical tip is to include explicit --url and --keypair flags in scripts to make behavior deterministic. These steps let you quickly identify whether the problem is configuration, funding, or program logic. This hands-on lab simulates a complete local development workflow. First, start a local Solana validator which emulates a network on your machine. Then open a second terminal to run CLI commands. Configure the CLI to localhost with solana config set --url localhost, generate a new keypair file for your local wallet, and set it as your default keypair. Request a generous localhost airdrop such as 100 SOL for testing, and verify the balance with solana balance. Create a recipient keypair, and send 50 SOL using the allow-unfunded-recipient flag to create the recipient account automatically. Copy the transfer's transaction signature and inspect it with solana transaction to view instruction logs and account changes. When finished, stop the local validator. This lab gives you a repeatable, safe environment for testing program logic and transactions without connecting to remote clusters. Beyond basic wallet and transfer commands, the CLI supports deploying compiled BPF programs and more advanced operations. The solana program deploy command uploads a compiled program file to the network; this assumes you have already built your program into a shared object file. While this chapter does not step through a full program deploy, it is important to know the CLI is the same entry point for deployments and program management. After deployment, the CLI still helps by showing deployed program addresses and by enabling transaction inspection to view program logs. Advanced troubleshooting often involves reading program logs and verifying that the program ID, accounts, and instruction data match your expectations. The CLI gives you the raw tools to inspect these elements. When you prepare to deploy, practice the local and devnet flows first so you understand account funding, program upgrade paths, and configuration flags used by the deploy command. Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. First, the Solana CLI is your direct interface to the network, enabling configuration, funding, transfers, and transaction inspection. Second, clusters matter: select mainnet-beta for production, devnet for public testing, testnet for validator testing, and localhost for local experiments; always confirm your URL and keypair. Third, airdrops provide test SOL on devnet and localhost and must be verified by signature and balance checks. Fourth, transfers require you to plan for transaction fees and sometimes to use the allow-unfunded-recipient flag when creating new recipient accounts. Finally, for debugging, always copy transaction signatures and inspect them with solana transaction to view instruction logs. Holding these rules as habits will make your development and debugging workflow deterministic and safer. Keep three compact reminders in mind as you work with the CLI. First, always confirm context: verify your cluster URL and default keypair before running commands. Second, plan for costs: check balances and include transaction fees, and use the allow-unfunded-recipient flag deliberately. Third, inspect transactions: copy signatures and use solana transaction to read program logs and instruction details. These three habits address the majority of common problems you will face while developing: accidental mainnet usage, insufficient funds, and opaque failures. If you practice this routine — verify, plan, inspect — you will shorten debugging cycles and avoid costly mistakes on shared networks.
